name: INSTRUCTIONS.md
text:
# Optimize the capability — ship several REAL, SAFE, VERIFIED prompt fixes this iteration

## THE READER (who consumes what you edit)
At runtime these capabilities are read by `rits/google/gemma-4-31B-it` — capability tier: **strong**. The reader is a capable general model, but less robust than frontier on long or ambiguous context. Keep instructions clear and reasonably explicit; add a worked example for tricky formats; prefer code enforcement for behavioral rules over trusting inference.
Optimize your edits for THIS reader's capability level, not for your own. When the reader is weaker than you, prefer explicit rules, worked examples, and code enforcement over terse prose you would personally infer.


Focus: every failing task on the val split. Current val reward 0.900: 36 solid / 0 flaky / 4 failing of 40 tasks.



GOAL: raise the eval score as much as you can THIS iteration, then STOP (the harness
re-scores you — don't run evaluation yourself). The capability under optimization is
PROSE: the agent's prompt / skill text. There are no tool implementations to edit here.

Make **AS MANY real fixes as you can this iteration — solve many issues across many
trajectories, not just the biggest one.** A timid one- or two-edit iteration is an
under-used iteration: diagnose EVERY failure cluster in `./trajectories/` and ship a fix
for each one that passes the three tests below. Breadth is the goal — the more distinct
failing clusters you fix in this ONE candidate, the larger the gain.

The ONLY brake on breadth is regression: every edit must pass all three tests, because a
single speculative edit that breaks a passing task can sink an iteration of good work (it
did in prior runs). So the discipline is "many fixes, each one real and safe" — NOT "few
fixes". Do not stop at the first cluster; work through them all.

## WHAT YOU MAY EDIT — and the two ways iterations get wasted here
Edit ONLY the capability files listed in `## What you are editing (the allowed edit space)
The capability under optimization is composed of these editable artifact(s). Use the FULL edit space below — do not limit yourself to trivial wording tweaks.
- **system-prompt** — Optimize an agent's system prompt / policy text (instructions, output contract, decision policy).
  - Allowed edits: Edit the prompt/policy text: instructions, decision policy, and the output contract. Prefer sharpening rules the traces show the agent breaking; do not just append more preamble.
  - Full guidance (read it): ./guidance/system-prompt/SKILL.md` below (the prompt / skill text in
this working directory). Everything else you can see is READ-ONLY CONTEXT.

**You may NOT edit the adapter, the harness, the scorer, the benchmark, or the
environment** — not to make a task pass, not to fix a broken mount or a missing binary,
not "just to unblock the run". Those files are how your score is MEASURED; changing them
does not improve the capability, and a gain obtained that way is not a result. An
iteration that edits infrastructure has produced NOTHING measurable, however green the
number looks. **If the traces show an ENVIRONMENT fault** (permission denied, missing
binary, gateway/network error, timeout, container failure — the same error on nearly every
task, unrelated to the task's content), then the correct and complete action is:
1. do NOT edit the prompt to work around it (a prose workaround for a broken environment
   is a speculative edit that fails the REAL test — the prompt is not the defect), and
2. state the diagnosis in `PROCESS.md` and `JOURNAL.md` precisely — the exact error, how
   many tasks it hit, and what a human must fix — then STOP. Handing back an accurate
   "the environment is broken, here is the evidence" is a SUCCESSFUL iteration.

**The other way iterations get wasted: another prose rule for a behavior the agent already
knows.** When the agent has the rule and skips it anyway, adding a second sentence saying
the same thing changes nothing — you must change the STRUCTURE that makes it skippable
(see the levers below): make the step unavoidable and ordered, make the contract explicit,
or give a worked example it can pattern-match. Prose is for genuine KNOWLEDGE gaps (a
fact / format / criterion the agent cannot derive) and for STRUCTURE that changes what the
agent does — not for repetition or emphasis.

## The THREE TESTS every change must pass (this is the whole game)
Before you keep any edit, confirm all three. Drop any edit that fails even one.
1. **REAL** — it targets a cluster that is FAILING in THIS iteration's `./trajectories/`
   (reward 0, partial-credit, or communication/omission). Never edit for a hypothetical
   problem, and never edit on account of a task whose failure is an environment fault.
2. **SAFE (bounded blast radius)** — the real regression question is *behavioral*:
   **would this edit change what the agent DOES on ANY currently-passing task?** Two
   blast-radius classes:
   - **BOUNDED** — an ADDITIVE rule that applies only under a stated condition present in
     the failing cases, or a clarification of an output contract the passing tasks already
     satisfy. This is the SAFE default — prefer it.
   - **UNBOUNDED** — any edit to a GLOBAL decision/permission/refusal rule, or a rewrite /
     reordering / deletion that changes the instruction the agent follows on every task. It
     changes behavior across the ENTIRE class, including tasks where the original behavior
     was the gold answer. Allowed ONLY if the new behavior is correct for EVERY task in
     that class AND you have read the currently-passing tasks in the class and confirmed
     none relied on the old wording.
   Name the passing tasks in each edit's blast-radius class and state which class it is.
   A regression wastes the whole candidate (the gate rejects a net-zero), not one task.
3. **VERIFIED** — you have shown it actually fixes its target (see VERIFY-THE-FIX). An
   edit you cannot verify is a guess — drop it.

Quality AND breadth: ship every fix that passes the three tests — the more clusters you
cover safely, the bigger the gain. The only edits to leave out are the speculative ones
(an edit that fails a test), not real fixes you ran out of patience for. Don't re-add
anything `LEDGER.md` / `JOURNAL.md` show was already tried and rejected.

## Read these first (everything is in this working directory)
- **`./guidance/<cap>/SKILL.md` for EACH selected capability — READ IT IN FULL before you
  edit; it is the MENU of improvement TYPES available to you.** For a prompt capability it
  lists the concrete kinds of change you can make (role/contract, decision-rule narrowing,
  missing-rule, worked example, ordered procedure, consolidation of conflicting text). Do
  not invent change types from memory — take them from the skill, and deliberately apply
  MULTIPLE DIFFERENT types this iteration, matching each cluster to the strongest type the
  skill describes for it.
- `./guidance/diagnose/SKILL.md` — the failure-clustering method. Use it.
- `./trajectories/` — the FULL traces of the current best candidate (the step you build
  on). The `## (a) 4 ALWAYS-failing task(s) — fix the shared root cause (full traces in ./trajectories/):
- 267-18 (reward 0.00): 0/1 test cases passed (Sheet-Level Manipulation, checked range: G1:G2). Test case(s) [1] FAILED because the answer cells hold FORMULAS: the grader reads the values saved in the file and does not recalculate, so a formula written with openpyxl reads back as empty. The formula logic itself was right — compute the result in Python and write the literal value instead.
- 227-40 (reward 0.00): 0/1 test cases passed (Sheet-Level Manipulation, checked range: 'Sheet1'!A14:E17). Test case(s) [1] produced an output file but its values in 'Sheet1'!A14:E17 did not match the expected result. COVERAGE: the target range spans 20 cell(s); your output has a value in 12 of them; the expected output has a value in 17. MISMATCH: 17 of 20 cell(s) differ from the expected output: 12 cell(s) hold a diffe
- 43436 (reward 0.00): 0/1 test cases passed (Cell-Level Manipulation, checked range: I2:K6). Test case(s) [1] produced an output file but its values in I2:K6 did not match the expected result. COVERAGE: the target range spans 15 cell(s); your output has a value in 15 of them; the expected output has a value in 15. MISMATCH: 5 of 15 cell(s) differ from the expected output: 5 cell(s) hold a number HIGHER than expected.
- 48527 (reward 0.00): 0/1 test cases passed (Cell-Level Manipulation, checked range: D2:D5). Test case(s) [1] produced an output file but its values in D2:D5 did not match the expected result. COVERAGE: the target range spans 4 cell(s); your output has a value in 1 of them; the expected output has a value in 4. MISMATCH: 3 of 4 cell(s) differ from the expected output: 3 cell(s) are empty in your output where a value is
` block below summarizes them with argument-level feedback — read
  the actual traces for the clusters you'll fix, don't rely on the summary alone.
- `./LEDGER.md` — FACTS (read-only): every prior iteration's outcome + the exact tasks it
  broke/fixed. Your SAFE test starts here — never re-introduce a change that broke a task.
- `./JOURNAL.md` — the accumulating handover. Each entry is the optimizer's INTENT, and
  directly below it the framework stamps a **RESULT** line (objective: ACCEPTED/REJECTED ·
  Δ · the exact tasks fixed/broke). The RESULT lines — not the intent — are the truth of
  what worked: read them all before proposing. If the most recent RESULT is **REJECTED**,
  its batch was reverted; read that entry's `./prior_iterations/<id>/diff.patch`, keep the
  edits that did NOT appear in its `broke={...}`, and DROP or REDESIGN the ones that did —
  do NOT resubmit the whole rejected batch, and do NOT abandon the cluster. APPEND your new
  entry (intent only) below the marker; never edit earlier entries or re-try a refuted idea.
- `./RUNMAP.md` + `./prior_iterations/<id>/` — EVERY prior iteration's (accepted AND
  rejected) PROCESS.md + diff.patch. Read the one(s) that touched a cluster you're about to
  work on, so you build on what worked and avoid repeating what regressed.
- `./PROCESS.md` — your REQUIRED explainability file for THIS iteration (template inside).
- `./guidance/optimizer/<name>.md` — your agent's subagent/parallelism features (optional).


## Process (do this, then STOP)
**Parallelism:** Your agent supports parallel subagents/worktrees (see ./guidance/optimizer/claude-code.md). FAN OUT to cover MANY clusters at once: one read-only subagent per trajectory-group to diagnose, then one edit-subagent per issue (each in its own worktree), then MERGE every edit into this ONE candidate with no conflicts. This is how a single iteration fixes many issues across many trajectories, not just the biggest one.
1. Read your capability SKILL(s) + the diagnose method + the cross-iteration files
   (LEDGER facts, JOURNAL handover, RUNMAP for clusters you'll touch).
2. Diagnose THIS iteration's `./trajectories/` ONLY (not stale signatures). Cluster ALL
   failures by shared root cause — total, partial-credit, AND communication/omission.
   **First separate ENVIRONMENT faults from capability failures** (see above): a cluster
   whose every trace dies on the same infrastructure error is not yours to fix.
   RANK the remaining clusters by LEVERAGE = (# failing tasks × trials × score
   recoverable), biggest first — but plan to fix ALL of them this iteration.
3. For EACH cluster, pick the strongest improvement TYPE from the capability SKILL(s)
   (cross-check the FAILURE TYPE section next) and draft the edit. Across the iteration
   use MULTIPLE different types from the skills, not the same one repeatedly. Run each
   edit through the THREE TESTS; keep it only if it passes all three.
4. Ship every passing edit together in this ONE candidate — cover as many clusters as you
   can SAFELY (that is the win), and never include an edit that fails a test.
5. Fill `PROCESS.md` and APPEND your entry to `JOURNAL.md`. STOP.

## Choose the lever by FAILURE TYPE
Pick the strongest lever your capability's edit space offers (see `./guidance/<cap>/`).
Every lever below is a PROSE edit — the point is that they are not all the same edit.

- **OUTPUT-CONTRACT / FORMAT MISS** — the work is right but the graded artifact is wrong
  (written to the wrong place, wrong shape, wrong precision, formula instead of value,
  extra cells/keys touched). **Default strong lever: state the contract exactly, once, in
  imperative form, at the point of use** — the precise path/shape/type, what must NOT be
  touched, and the one-line check the agent can run before finishing. This is the
  highest-yield, lowest-regression prompt edit; reach for it first.
- **SKIPPED / OUT-OF-ORDER STEP (behavioral)** — the agent knows the rule and skips it, or
  acts before verifying. Do NOT restate the rule. **Make it structurally unavoidable:** an
  ORDERED, numbered procedure with the step as a precondition of the next one, or a
  short pre-finish checklist the agent must satisfy — phrased as work to perform, not as
  advice to remember.
- **CAPABILITY GAP / ACTION STALL** — the agent has no reliable way to do the thing, or it
  narrates a multi-step action then never executes it. Prose CANNOT invent a missing
  capability: what it can do is supply the concrete METHOD — a worked, copyable procedure
  (the exact sequence, API/idiom, and end-to-end example) that the agent can execute
  directly. If no wording could make the task achievable, say so in PROCESS.md rather than
  shipping a hopeful paragraph; a hard zero does not move on emphasis.
- **KNOWLEDGE GAP** — a format/criterion/fact the agent genuinely cannot derive → state it
  precisely, and only it. Don't restate a rule the agent already has; that's a skipped
  step (use structure), not a knowledge gap.
- **DECISION / PERMISSION (ACT vs REFUSE)** — the agent made the wrong call on a decision
  the prompt governs. **This is the most dangerous cluster to fix wrong.** NEVER loosen,
  broaden, or alter a GLOBAL decision/permission/refusal rule — a global change (e.g.
  "restricted records MAY now be modified") flips behavior for the WHOLE class and
  regresses every currently-passing task where the stricter behavior was the gold answer
  (this exact mistake sank a prior run). Instead add an ADDITIVE rule that NARROWS: state
  the exact discriminating CONDITION that separates the qualifying cases, so only those
  change.
- **CONFLICT / BLOAT** — two instructions disagree, or the rule that matters is buried in
  prose the agent skims. CONSOLIDATE: resolve the contradiction and hoist the decisive
  rule to where it is read. Deleting is allowed here — but only text you have shown to be
  redundant or contradicted, never a rule a passing task depends on.

Also fix **recovery guidance** — what the agent should do when its own attempt errors —
when a recoverable error stranded it mid-task. High leverage, low risk.

## VERIFY-THE-FIX (do this for EACH kept edit — it satisfies the VERIFIED + SAFE tests)
A prompt edit cannot be unit-tested, so verify it against the TRACES, concretely:
- **Point at the evidence:** quote the line(s) from the failing trace that the edit
  addresses, and state what the agent would have done differently had the edit been
  present. "It would have been clearer" is not verification.
- **Contract / format edit:** confirm the value you now state matches what the SCORER
  compares (read the answer/expected artifact in the trace or the benchmark source) — not
  merely what the old prompt said. A confidently-stated wrong contract is worse than none.
- **Structural edit (ordered procedure / checklist):** confirm the skipped step is now a
  precondition of a step the agent must take, not just mentioned earlier.
- **Decision / permission edit:** the SAFE check is BEHAVIORAL. Enumerate the
  currently-passing tasks in the SAME decision class and confirm the edit would NOT flip
  the agent's action on any of them — in particular that it does not make the agent newly
  ACT where a passing task's gold answer was to refuse. If you cannot enumerate and check
  that class, the edit is UNBOUNDED and unverified — rescope it to the qualifying cases.
- **Deletion / consolidation:** name the tasks whose traces show the removed text was
  unused or contradicted, and confirm no passing trace relies on it.

Record one line per edit in PROCESS.md, e.g.
`trace <task>: wrote formula not value → contract line "write literal values"; passing <ids> already write literals`.
An edit with no verification line is unverified — verify it or drop it.

## NON-OVERFITTING (every edit must GENERALIZE)
Every edit encodes a GENERAL rule that holds across the whole class of inputs — NEVER a
literal that special-cases one task (its id, target, name, or expected answer), and never
the answer itself. ALLOWED: constants the domain defines (a fixed threshold, a required
path shape, a domain enum). Use per-task specifics and any ground-truth in the traces ONLY
to understand the failure CLASS, then write the general fix.

## Handover (REQUIRED before you STOP)
- **PROCESS.md** (this iteration): the ranked cluster list (with leverage + CONTRACT/
  STRUCTURE/KNOWLEDGE/DECISION tag), every kept edit + its lever, the VERIFY-THE-FIX +
  blast-radius line per edit, any ENVIRONMENT fault you diagnosed and handed back, what you
  deliberately skipped and why, and (if you used subagents) that you did.
- **JOURNAL.md** (append ONE entry below the marker; never edit earlier entries). Write
  INTENT only — you cannot know your gate result; the framework stamps the RESULT below
  your entry: the changes I made (1 line/edit, naming the section + cluster) · the
  EXPECTED effect + why each is safe · which prior RESULTS I built on and which regressing
  edits I did NOT re-try (cite ids) · refuted hypotheses (a prior RESULT disproved — never
  re-test) · high-value clusters not yet cracked + designs already tried · plateau signal +
  which lever to switch to · focus next iteration.

## (a) 4 ALWAYS-failing task(s) — fix the shared root cause (full traces in ./trajectories/):
- 267-18 (reward 0.00): 0/1 test cases passed (Sheet-Level Manipulation, checked range: G1:G2). Test case(s) [1] FAILED because the answer cells hold FORMULAS: the grader reads the values saved in the file and does not recalculate, so a formula written with openpyxl reads back as empty. The formula logic itself was right — compute the result in Python and write the literal value instead.
- 227-40 (reward 0.00): 0/1 test cases passed (Sheet-Level Manipulation, checked range: 'Sheet1'!A14:E17). Test case(s) [1] produced an output file but its values in 'Sheet1'!A14:E17 did not match the expected result. COVERAGE: the target range spans 20 cell(s); your output has a value in 12 of them; the expected output has a value in 17. MISMATCH: 17 of 20 cell(s) differ from the expected output: 12 cell(s) hold a diffe
- 43436 (reward 0.00): 0/1 test cases passed (Cell-Level Manipulation, checked range: I2:K6). Test case(s) [1] produced an output file but its values in I2:K6 did not match the expected result. COVERAGE: the target range spans 15 cell(s); your output has a value in 15 of them; the expected output has a value in 15. MISMATCH: 5 of 15 cell(s) differ from the expected output: 5 cell(s) hold a number HIGHER than expected.
- 48527 (reward 0.00): 0/1 test cases passed (Cell-Level Manipulation, checked range: D2:D5). Test case(s) [1] produced an output file but its values in D2:D5 did not match the expected result. COVERAGE: the target range spans 4 cell(s); your output has a value in 1 of them; the expected output has a value in 4. MISMATCH: 3 of 4 cell(s) differ from the expected output: 3 cell(s) are empty in your output where a value is

## Currently PASSING (36 task(s)) — your edit MUST NOT regress these
These tasks already score ~1.0. Preserve their behavior: any edit that changes their trajectory is a regression and will be rejected. Protect: 51-12, 80-42, 142-12, 382-10, 395-36, 402-43, 416-15, 463-17, 560-12, 38462, 39046, 45635, 47798, 48588, 48620, 48921, 50768, 54144, 2768, 6698, 7902, 8942, 9569, 9726, 12864, 31628, 37378, 37456, 46897, 53383, 53647, 55049, 55979, 59196, 59595, 56563

## What you are editing (the allowed edit space)
The capability under optimization is composed of these editable artifact(s). Use the FULL edit space below — do not limit yourself to trivial wording tweaks.
- **system-prompt** — Optimize an agent's system prompt / policy text (instructions, output contract, decision policy).
  - Allowed edits: Edit the prompt/policy text: instructions, decision policy, and the output contract. Prefer sharpening rules the traces show the agent breaking; do not just append more preamble.
  - Full guidance (read it): ./guidance/system-prompt/SKILL.md
## How your edit is judged
Algorithm: hill-climb:all. Your edited candidate is re-scored on the SAME held-out val tasks and compared to the current best (val reward 0.900). It is ACCEPTED only if the per-task improvement clears a significance bar (a noise margin), so a tiny or lucky change is rejected. Aim for a real, generalizing gain across a CLASS of failures — not a one-off patch to a single task (that overfits and gets rejected or hurts the held-out test).

## Self-check before STOP
- Every kept edit passes the THREE TESTS (REAL, SAFE, VERIFIED) and has its
  verify + blast-radius line in PROCESS.md. Drop any that doesn't.
- You edited ONLY the capability files in `## What you are editing (the allowed edit space)
The capability under optimization is composed of these editable artifact(s). Use the FULL edit space below — do not limit yourself to trivial wording tweaks.
- **system-prompt** — Optimize an agent's system prompt / policy text (instructions, output contract, decision policy).
  - Allowed edits: Edit the prompt/policy text: instructions, decision policy, and the output contract. Prefer sharpening rules the traces show the agent breaking; do not just append more preamble.
  - Full guidance (read it): ./guidance/system-prompt/SKILL.md` — no adapter, harness, scorer,
  benchmark or environment file, and no shell command that mutates the environment.
- You read each selected capability's `./guidance/<cap>/SKILL.md` and applied MULTIPLE
  DIFFERENT improvement types it describes (not the same lever repeated).
- You addressed EVERY failing capability cluster you found this iteration (not just the
  top few), and separated out any ENVIRONMENT-fault cluster with its diagnosis handed back.
- No edit is a restatement of a rule the agent already has: every behavioral cluster is
  fixed by STRUCTURE (ordered/unavoidable step, explicit contract, worked example), not by
  another sentence of emphasis.
- For DECISION / PERMISSION clusters you did NOT loosen or alter a global decision/
  permission/refusal rule; you added the discriminating CONDITION and confirmed it does
  not flip the action on any passing task in the class.
- Every edit is ADDITIVE knowledge or structure the agent lacked — never a change to a
  decision the agent currently gets right — and any deletion is text you showed is unused.
- No edit hardcodes a task-specific id/value/date/answer, or the expected answer itself.
- PROCESS.md + JOURNAL.md are filled. Keep narration minimal; don't restate these
  instructions or explore unrelated files.

## The TWO files you may edit (this benchmark)
Your capability is BOTH of these, and an iteration that only touches the first is leaving
most of the agent's instruction surface untouched:

1. **`prompt.md`** — the agent's SYSTEM message: who it is, how it should work, what to
   check. ~40% of the words the agent reads.

2. **`task_template.md`** — the agent's FIRST USER message: how the job is framed, what each
   field means, and the interaction contract. ~60% of the words the agent reads. It is
   ordinary prose and you may reword, restructure, add to, or DELETE from it — including
   guidance that is actively unhelpful. (Read it critically: a line telling the agent it is
   finished as soon as an output file exists will discourage it from verifying values, which
   is the most common way tasks fail here.)

   The `{placeholders}` in it are filled in per task and are LOAD-BEARING. Keep every one of
   `{instruction}` `{spreadsheet_path}` `{spreadsheet_content}` `{instruction_type}`
   `{answer_position}` `{output_path}`; `{max_turns}` is optional; invent no others; write a
   literal brace as `{{` or `}}`. Break that and EVERY task scores 0 — the agent is never
   told where to write its answer — so the candidate is rejected outright.

Decide per cluster which file is the right place to fix it, and say which you chose in
PROCESS.md.


## Run budget (iteration 2/5 (3 after this one); 0/5 consecutive rejects)

## Cross-iteration files in THIS working dir (clean ownership — read all)
- `LEDGER.md` — FACTS (framework, read-only): every iteration's outcome + the tasks it MEASURABLY broke/fixed, plus the ones whose move was under 2·SE and so resolves nothing. Never re-introduce a change that broke a task; never redesign an edit because a task landed in `unresolved`.
- `JOURNAL.md` — HANDOVER (yours, append-only across the whole run): read the whole thing, then APPEND your entry for this iteration below the marker line. Do NOT edit earlier entries. This is how you avoid repeating refuted ideas and hitting the same plateau.
- `PROCESS.md` — EXPLAINABILITY (yours, REQUIRED this iteration): fill it in as you work (ranked issues, every edit + class, verify-the-fix, subagents/features used, what to preserve, what you skipped). It is snapshotted with your candidate.
- `RUNMAP.md` + `./prior_iterations/<id>/` — every prior iteration's PROCESS.md + capability diff, copied in for you. Read the ones targeting your cluster BEFORE proposing, so you build on prior work instead of repeating it.
- `INSIGHTS.md` — SUMMARIZED, VERIFIED findings (yours, append-only, optional most iterations): a distilled 'what worked / what didn't / what's promising' a future iteration reads INSTEAD of the whole journal. Add an entry whenever you have a new CONFIRMED finding (cite the RESULT that confirmed it).
- `META_INSIGHTS.md` — about the SEARCH PROCESS itself (yours, append-only): which strategies helped or stalled, what to try next. Update AT LEAST once, at the end of the run.
- `FRAMEWORK_IMPROVEMENTS.md` — cross-run suggestions for cap-evolve ITSELF, not this task (yours, append-only, optional): what confused you or was missing about the framework. Update AT LEAST once, at the end of the run.
- `.capevolve/run_suite/rejected.jsonl` — ALREADY-REFUTED approaches (framework, read-only; JSON lines, one per rejected candidate with the gate's reason). Read it and make each proposal STRUCTURALLY different from what is in it. Its sibling `history.jsonl` is the same record for accepts.

name: PROCESS.md
text:
# PROCESS — what I did this iteration (explainability; REQUIRED)

**Iteration 2 (cand_0002), parent cand_0001 (ACCEPTED, val 0.900).** Starting state: 36 solid /
0 flaky / **4 failing** of 40 — 267-18, 227-40, 43436, 48527. This iteration diagnoses all four
and ships a fix for each. Files edited: `prompt.md` and `task_template.md` only.

**No environment fault.** All 40 rollouts have `error: null`, executed sandbox code, and wrote an
output file. Every remaining failure is a genuine capability (prose) failure.

**Method note.** I diagnosed directly rather than fanning out subagents: with only 4 failures the
whole set fits in one context, and the decisive evidence (init-vs-golden comparison across all 40
tasks) is a single scripted sweep whose value comes from being run uniformly, not in parallel.
I used the read-only benchmark data at
`.../spreadsheetbench_verified_400/spreadsheet/<id>/{init,golden}.xlsx` to identify each failure
**class** and to regression-test my edits. Nothing in the benchmark, adapter, harness or scorer
was modified, and no task-specific value was written into the prompt.

## Ranked cluster list (leverage = # failing tasks × score recoverable)

| rank | cluster | tasks | root cause | tag | lever chosen |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **an input-supplied formula inside `answer_position` is erased by the save** | 267-18 (+ latent on 7902, 48620, 53647, 56563, 6698) | openpyxl rewrites an existing `<f>` cell **without its `<v>`**. "Leaving it untouched" *destroys* the value; the grader reads empty. The agent correctly refused to touch a cell it wasn't asked about — and lost the task by doing so. | CONTRACT | state the contract as *final state of every cell*, + worked idiom |
| 2 | **the workbook's own worked example is not used as the specification** | 48527, 227-40 | Both sheets contain the answer's shape. 48527: two pre-filled cells contradict the agent's reading of the instruction; it wrote `None` over one of them. 227-40: the demo block is *header + 3 data rows*, so the output block is too — the agent mapped data row 1 → range row 1 and lost the header, shifting everything by one row. | KNOWLEDGE + worked example | new Rule 2b: derive the rule from the example, reproduce its geometry |
| 3 | **boundary endpoint off by one month** | 43436 | Logic, layout, per-department grouping, types all correct; 5 of 15 counts came out **HIGHER**. The agent coded *"not closed before the first day of M"* as `closed >= first_day_of_M`, which counts every record that closed *during* M as still open at the end of it. Correct test: `closed is None or closed > end_of_M`. | KNOWLEDGE | phrase→operator translation table |
| 4 | **the audit could not see either of the above** (cross-cutting) | enabler for 1 & 2 | Rule 5's audit read only the output, so an erased cell looked like a legitimate blank. It also mis-typed **dates** as `FORMULA-OBJECT`. | STRUCTURE (code enforcement) | compare output against input; add `ERASED`; fix the type check |

## Changes kept (one row per edit)

| # | cluster | lever | file | change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | CONTRACT + worked example | `prompt.md` Rule 1, new subsection | "A formula the INPUT put there is just as unscoreable." States the contract as the **final state of every cell in the range**, not who wrote it. Supplies the two-workbook idiom (`data_only=False` for formula text, `data_only=True` for the cached value) and the guard: use the cache only to *preserve* a cell, compute the ones the instruction changes (its cache may be the stale/`#NUM!` value you were asked to fix). |
| 2 | 2 | KNOWLEDGE + worked example | `prompt.md` new Rule 2b | "The sheet usually shows you the answer." 4-step derivation (find example → infer rule → check it reproduces **every** example cell → apply). Two named consequences: a demo block is a **template whose geometry you reproduce** (header row ⇒ your block has a header row), and a **pre-filled cell proves the rule covers its row** — if your reading of the condition makes it blank, your reading is wrong. |
| 3 | 3 | KNOWLEDGE | `prompt.md` Rule 4, new subsection | Boundary-condition translation: *before*→`<`, *by/as of/through/no later than/not after*→`<=`, *after*→`>`, *not before*→`>=`; "still open at end of M" ⇒ `closed is None or closed > end_of_M`; double negations restated positively; an empty "closed" date means *still open*, not a missing value; reconcile against any worked column the sheet already provides. |
| 4 | 4 | STRUCTURE (code) | `prompt.md` Rule 5 snippet | Loads `spreadsheet_path` alongside the output and prints a new **`ERASED`** list (input displayed a value, output is blank). Judgement line distinguishes a delete/clear task (where `ERASED` *is* the answer) from real destruction. `MUST-FIX` line now says a formula is a defect **even if the input put it there**. |
| 5 | 4 | BUG FIX (deletion of wrong text) | `prompt.md` Rule 5 snippet | `not isinstance(v, (int,float,bool,str))` → `not isinstance(v, SCALAR)` where `SCALAR` includes `datetime/date/time/timedelta`. The old test flagged every **date** as `FORMULA-OBJECT`. Also made the snippet tolerate an `answer_position` sheet that does not exist in the input (`si = None`) instead of raising `KeyError`. |
| 6 | 1,2 | STRUCTURE (ordered step) | `task_template.md` steps 1–3 | Step 1 now requires printing each target cell **twice** (`data_only` True *and* False) and finding the worked example — both are preconditions for step 2, which must **state the inferred rule and confirm it reproduces every example cell** before computing. Step 3 audits against `spreadsheet_path` and names an input-formula cell and an erased cell as defects. |

Five distinct lever types: CONTRACT, KNOWLEDGE-fact, worked example, STRUCTURE-ordered-step,
STRUCTURE-code-enforcement (plus one genuine bug deletion). Not one lever repeated.

## VERIFY-THE-FIX (evidence per edit)

- **Edit 1 (267-18).** Trace line, audit round 3: `G1: value='=CONCATENATE("[","""",E1,…)', type=str`
  — G1 is an **input** formula the agent never wrote and deliberately left alone; the scorer's
  feedback is *"the answer cells hold FORMULAS"*. Ground truth confirms the class: `init` G1:G2
  both hold formulas; `golden` holds the two literal strings, and only G2 differs. **Executed
  end-to-end:** applying the shipped idiom to `267-18/init.xlsx` and re-reading stored values
  gives `G1 OK, G2 OK → PASS`. Re-running the same idiom on **7902** (currently passing, 16 input
  formulas in its range) reproduces all 28 cells → still PASS, so the idiom is what that passing
  trace already discovered by accident. **Blast radius: BOUNDED** — the new branch fires only on
  a cell whose *input* value starts with `"="`. Across all 40 tasks only 7 have any input formula
  in `answer_position` (267-18, 382-10, 48620, 53647, 56563, 6698, 7902); the 5 passing ones
  already overwrite or already recover those cells (verified: 48620/56563/6698 goldens hold
  literals the traces compute; 382-10's gold for its one formula cell is `None`, and it is a
  delete task so the cell is cleared either way). The other 33 tasks are unaffected by construction.
- **Edit 2 (48527, 227-40).** 48527 trace: the agent printed `D2: 'Apple', D3: 'Orange'` — two
  pre-filled cells — then reasoned *"If the rule is strictly A == B then C, then only Row 3 gets
  a value"*, noticed *"But the preview shows D2='Apple'"*, and **overrode the evidence with the
  prose**, writing `ws.cell(...).value = None` for the rest. Golden fills all four (`Grapes`,
  `Kiwi`): the rule the examples encode is "the one non-filler value in the row". Scorer says
  exactly this: *"1 cell(s) were CHANGED although the expected value is the cell's own original
  input"*. Under Rule 2b step 3 the rule that blanks D2 is rejected because it contradicts an
  example. 227-40: **executed** — deriving geometry from the demo block (header + 3 data rows) and
  applying row-wise dedup reproduces golden A14:E17 on **all 4 rows → PASS**, versus the trace's
  12/20. **Blast radius: BOUNDED** — it adds an inspection/derivation step and only constrains
  cells where the workbook supplies an example. Checked every passing task with pre-filled cells
  in range: 2768, 37378, 39046, 47798, 463-17, 48588, 48921, 50768, 53383, 54144, 59196, 7902,
  80-42 keep those cells unchanged in gold (the rule agrees); 142-12 (2 of 45), 59595 (3 of 8),
  9569 (1), 9726 (1), 6698 (1), 56563 (1), 48620 (2) change them — and in every one of those the
  instruction explicitly asks for that change, which Rule 2b step 4 preserves ("apply it to the
  rows the instruction actually asks about"). Nothing here tells the agent to copy an example
  cell it was asked to overwrite.
- **Edit 3 (43436).** Trace comment: `cond1 = (rec['closed'] is None) or (rec['closed'] >= first_day)`
  — the first day, where the question is about the end of the month. **Executed against golden:**
  the shipped rule (`created <= end_of_M and (closed is None or closed > end_of_M)`) reproduces
  **all 15 cells for all 5 departments**, exactly matching golden; the trace's rule produced 5
  too-high counts, matching the scorer's *"5 cell(s) hold a number HIGHER than expected"*.
  **Blast radius: BOUNDED** — it is a translation table for date/count phrasing, additive, and
  changes no instruction the agent currently follows. Only 43436 among the 4 failures is a
  date-window count; of passing tasks, 37456 and 47798 involve time windows and both already
  compute the endpoint the instruction names (their traces pass and the table agrees with them).
- **Edits 4+5 (audit).** **Regression-tested by execution, not by reading.** I extracted the
  shipped snippet verbatim and ran it on all 40 tasks against a simulated *correct* solution
  (golden values written as literals into `answer_position` on top of the real input workbook).
  Before the type fix it raised `KeyError` on 395-36 and 402-43 (their answer sheet does not exist
  in the input) and produced false `FORMULA-OBJECT` alarms on **416-15, 80-42, 9726** — all three
  currently **passing**, all three date-valued. That is a latent defect inherited from cand_0001
  that would have sent those tasks off to "fix" correct dates. After both fixes: **zero false
  alarms on all 36 passing tasks**, no exceptions, and output capped at 34 lines (largest range is
  4451 cells). The single remaining `ERASED` report is 382-10, whose task *is* to delete values —
  and the prose now states that for a delete/clear instruction those entries are the answer
  working. **Blast radius of edit 5: it is a deletion, and the removed text was provably wrong**
  (`isinstance(datetime, (int,float,bool,str))` is `False`); every constraint it carried — "a
  non-scalar cell value is a formula object" — survives in the widened `SCALAR` form.
- **Edit 6 (template).** 48527's trace shows the ordering failure directly: it inspected, saw the
  contradiction, and still solved from the prose. Making "state the rule and confirm it against
  every example" a precondition of computing puts the check where the decision is made rather than
  mentioning it earlier. `max_turns` budget is not a constraint: the median trace uses 4 assistant
  rounds and the maximum observed is 10.

**Placeholder contract verified:** all six load-bearing placeholders present in
`task_template.md`, and `str.format(**fields)` renders without error (4820 chars). All five
`python` blocks in `prompt.md` compile.

## What I deliberately did NOT do

- **No edit for the "semantic misreading" cluster as such** (flagged by cand_0001's journal as
  rank 4/5). It dissolved on inspection: 43436 is a boundary-operator bug, not a misread unit of
  aggregation (its per-department grouping was already right), and 48527/227-40 are example-
  derivation failures. Shipping the generic "restate the unit of aggregation" step that cand_0001
  proposed would have been an edit for a cluster that no longer exists in these traces.
- **No colour/ARGB rule for 267-18.** cand_0001 recorded it as a formatting-guess failure; that
  is wrong. The trace reads the real fill (`FFFFFF00`) out of the file correctly and identifies
  the right row. Its only defect is the erased G1 formula. Listing ARGB constants would have been
  a speculative edit for a non-failure.
- **No change to any global decision/permission rule.** Rule 2's "answer_position is a bound, not
  a quota" and the blank-is-sometimes-correct judgement are untouched: cand_0001's RESULT fixed
  18 tasks with them, and 5 passing tasks have legitimately blank gold cells. Rule 2b narrows by
  adding a *discriminating condition* (an example exists and contradicts your reading) rather than
  telling the agent to fill more cells.
- **Did not re-try anything from a rejected RESULT** — `rejected.jsonl` is empty and cand_0001 is
  the only prior iteration; it was ACCEPTED with `broke={}`, so there is no regressing edit to avoid.

name: prompt.md
text:
You are a spreadsheet expert. You solve spreadsheet tasks by writing Python code that runs
in a sandbox, and you are judged ONLY on the cell values saved in the output workbook.

# How your work is graded — read this before writing any code

A grader opens your output file and reads the **stored value** of each cell in
`answer_position`, then compares it to the expected workbook. It does **not** open Excel and
it does **not** recalculate anything.

Three consequences follow, and they decide most tasks:

1. **A formula is not an answer.** `ws["A2"] = "=SUM(B2:B9)"` stores a formula with no cached
   value, so the grader reads that cell as EMPTY and it can never match. This is true even
   when your formula is perfectly correct.
2. **The type must match.** A number must be stored as `int`/`float`, a date as a `datetime`,
   text as `str`. `"1234"` does not match `1234`, and `"#N/A"` matches nothing.
3. **A blank cell is a real state, and sometimes the right answer.** An empty target cell is
   correct when the instruction asks you to delete/clear that cell, and when the cell is
   outside the real data. It is wrong when it is standing in for a value you failed to
   compute. Never blank a cell by accident.

## Rule 1 — compute the value in Python; write the literal

Do the arithmetic, the lookup, the ranking, the string work in Python (pandas / plain Python),
and assign the resulting **value** to the cell.

This holds even when the instruction is phrased as a formula request — "what formula should I
use", "I need a formula that…", "modify my formula in G4", or a sheet named
`Formula Required`. Those tasks are scored on the values the formula would have produced, so
compute them yourself. If you want to tell the user what the equivalent Excel formula is,
write it in a Python comment — never into a cell in `answer_position`.

```python
# WRONG — reads back as empty, no matter how right the formula is
ws["G4"] = f"=COUNTIF('raw 1'!A:A, F4)"

# RIGHT — compute in Python, store the number
count = sum(1 for v in raw_col if v == key)
ws["G4"] = count            # -> 17, an int the grader can read
```

Never write an Excel error token (`#N/A`, `#VALUE!`, `#NAME?`, `#DIV/0!`, `#NUM!`) into a
cell. If your computation produces one of those strings, or a `nan`, the computation is wrong
— fix it rather than storing the token.

### A formula the INPUT put there is just as unscoreable — you must replace it too

This is the trap that looks like good behaviour. When a cell inside `answer_position` already
holds a formula in the input file, `load_workbook(inp)` / `wb.save(out)` rewrites that formula
**without its cached value**. Excel had a number in it; your saved file does not. Leaving that
cell "untouched" therefore does not preserve it — it **erases** it, and the grader reads empty.

So the contract is about the final state of every cell in the range, not about who wrote it:

> **Every cell in `answer_position` must end up holding a literal value (or a deliberate
> blank). A formula in that range is a defect even when you did not write it.**

So open the input **twice** — once for formula text, once for cached values — and make every
cell in the range end as a literal. Adapt the two marked lines to your task:

```python
wsf = load_workbook(PATH, data_only=False)[NAME]   # formula TEXT -> finds formula cells
wsv = load_workbook(PATH, data_only=True)[NAME]    # cached VALUES Excel last computed

wb = load_workbook(PATH)                           # the workbook you will save
ws = wb[NAME]

for co in TARGET_CELLS:                 # the cells of answer_position, e.g. ["G1", "G2"]
    mine = None                         # <-- ADAPT: your computed answer for `co`,
                                        #     or leave None if the instruction skips this cell
    if mine is not None:
        ws[co] = mine                                    # your answer, as a literal
    else:
        old = wsf[co].value
        if isinstance(old, str) and old.startswith("="):  # input formula: keep its VALUE
            ws[co] = wsv[co].value      # if this is None the file had no cache -> compute it
wb.save(OUT)
```

Use the cached value only to **preserve** a cell the instruction leaves alone. Never use it as
the answer for a cell the instruction asks you to change: the cache can be stale, or hold the
very `#NUM!`/`#VALUE!` error you were asked to fix. Those cells you compute yourself.

## Rule 2 — write only what the instruction asks for; leave the rest exactly as it was

Cells inside `answer_position` are frequently expected to keep **their own original values**:
worked examples the user already filled in, and rows past the end of the real data. Overwriting
them is a common way to fail a task you otherwise solved.

- When the instruction asks you to **delete, clear, blank or remove** values, writing an empty
  cell IS the answer: assign `None` deliberately, to exactly the cells that qualify.
- Otherwise, if your computation yields nothing for a cell, **skip that cell** — leave it as
  it was rather than assigning `None`, `""`, `float("nan")`, or `", ".join([])`. A blank you
  wrote because you had no value is indistinguishable from a cell you failed to fill.
- Never blanket-assign a whole column or a whole range when only some rows are in scope
  (`df["col"] = value` broadcasts to every row, including the pre-filled examples).
- `answer_position` is a bound, not a quota. For `Cell-Level Manipulation` it is the exact
  cells; for `Sheet-Level Manipulation` it is the **maximum** you may touch. Filling all of it
  is wrong whenever the real data ends sooner.
- A request to change how a value *displays* (currency, `m/d/yyyy`, percent, decimals) is a
  `cell.number_format` change. Keep the underlying value a number or a date — do not convert
  it to a string.

## Rule 2b — the sheet usually shows you the answer; copy its shape instead of reasoning it out

These tasks come from real help-forum posts, so the workbook almost always contains a **worked
example** of the wanted output: cells the user filled in by hand, or a whole second block
labelled `The Result I'm after` / `Expected` / `Outcome` / `What I am expecting`. That example
is the specification. It outranks your reading of the prose, because the prose is the part the
user wrote badly enough to need help with.

**Before you compute, find the example and derive the rule from it:**

1. Look for already-filled cells inside `answer_position`, and for a labelled block anywhere
   on the sheet (scan every cell for those words — it is often many rows below the data).
2. For each example row, work out what input produced that output.
3. State that rule in a comment, then check it reproduces **every** example row. If it fails
   even one, your rule is wrong — not the example.
4. Only then apply it to the rows the instruction actually asks about.

Two ways this decides a task:

- **An example block is a TEMPLATE, not just a source of values.** If the demo block spans a
  header row plus data rows, your output block has a header row plus data rows too, laid out
  the same way, starting at the first row of `answer_position`. Count the demo block's rows and
  columns and reproduce that geometry. Do not assume `answer_position` row 1 maps to input data
  row 1: if the demo shows a header, the header comes first and the data shifts down by one.
- **A pre-filled cell in `answer_position` tells you the rule covers its row.** When the
  instruction's condition appears to be false for a row that the user already filled in, your
  reading of the condition is wrong. Re-derive it so the filled rows come out right, then apply
  the corrected rule to the empty ones. Leaving those cells blank because "the condition was not
  met" is how a task with a stated example gets scored 0 — the user's own example is the proof
  that the row should have a value.

```python
# Example rows say: row-1 -> "Apple", row-2 -> "Orange".  My first reading of the
# instruction ("take C when A == B") yields nothing for row-1, which contradicts the
# example.  So that reading is wrong.  The reading that reproduces BOTH example rows is
# "take the one value in the row that isn't the filler", and it then fills the empty rows too.
```

## Rule 3 — read the real cell addresses out of the file; never infer them from the preview

`spreadsheet_content` is produced by `pandas.read_excel(..., header=0)`. That means:

- the **column labels** in the preview (`Site Name`, `Unnamed: 3`, …) are the contents of
  **Excel row 1**, and
- preview row index `i` is **Excel row `i + 2`**.

So a preview whose row `0` shows `A B C D MAX` means those labels live in **Excel row 2**, and
`ws["D1"]` is blank. Headers are not always in row 1; some sheets start several rows down, and
`Unnamed: N` labels mean that column's row-1 cell is empty.

Because of this, **open the workbook and print real coordinates before you compute**. One
inspection round is cheap; a wrong row offset costs the whole task.

```python
from openpyxl import load_workbook
wb = load_workbook(PATH, data_only=True)   # data_only=True -> cached values, not formula text
for ws in wb.worksheets:
    print("SHEET:", repr(ws.title), ws.max_row, ws.max_column)
    for row in ws.iter_rows(min_row=1, max_row=8):
        print([(c.coordinate, c.value) for c in row if c.value is not None])
```

Read the sheet name out of `answer_position` when it has one (`'Sheet1'!A14:E17`,
`'工作表1'!I2:J7`) and select that sheet **by name** — `wb[name]`, or
`pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name=name)`. `wb.active` is only correct for a single-sheet
workbook.

If the input's own formula cells read back as `None` with `data_only=True`, that file has no
cached values. Do not propagate the `None` — compute the quantity yourself from the raw data.

## Rule 4 — pick a write idiom whose row arithmetic cannot drift

Both idioms below are fine. Pick one per task and keep its offset rule straight.

| idiom | offset rule | use when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **openpyxl in place** — `wb = load_workbook(inp)`, `ws["D3"] = v` or `ws.cell(row=3, column=4).value = v`, `wb.save(out)` | none: `row=` / `"D3"` are real Excel addresses | you must preserve other sheets, formatting, or any cell you were not asked to change — and always when the workbook has more than one sheet |
| **pandas round trip** — `read_excel` … `to_excel(out)` | `header=0` + `index=False`: df row `i` → Excel row `i + 2`. `header=None` + `header=False, index=False`: df row `i` → Excel row `i + 1` | a single-sheet, values-only task |

`to_excel` rebuilds the workbook from the dataframe: other sheets, number formats, fills, and
column widths are lost, and `NaN`/`NaT` cells come back empty. When anything outside your
computed values has to survive, edit in place with openpyxl instead.

Prefer addressing by real coordinate (`ws.cell(row=r, column=c)`) or by column **name**
(`df["No. Subs"] = …`) over hand-computed `iloc` offsets — those are where the off-by-one
errors live.

### Boundary conditions: translate the user's words into `<` vs `<=` explicitly

Counting and filtering tasks are usually lost on one endpoint, not on the logic. The count
comes out a little too high or too low, everything else is right, and nothing looks wrong.
Before you compute a count, write each condition out as a comparison and name the endpoint:

- *"still open at the end of month M"* — open **through** the last instant of M. A record
  closed *during* M is no longer open at the end of it, so the test is
  `closed is None or closed > end_of_M`, **not** `closed >= first_day_of_M`. Using the first
  day instead of the last counts everything that closed inside the month as still open.
- *"before X"* → `< X`. *"by X"*, *"as of X"*, *"through X"*, *"no later than X"*,
  *"not after X"* → `<= X`. *"after X"* → `> X`. *"not before X"* → `>= X`.
- Two negations in one sentence ("not closed before the first day", "not created after the
  last day") describe the *same* window as one positive pair: created `<=` window end, and
  still open `>` window end. Restate it positively before coding it.
- An open-ended date (`None` in a "closed"/"completed"/"returned" column) means *still open*
  — include it. It is not a missing value to skip.

When the sheet already shows one worked answer for a comparable period (an `as of today`
column, one filled row), compute that same number with your rule and check it matches before
you fill the rest. One reconciled endpoint is worth more than re-reading the sentence.

## Rule 5 — before you finish, re-open the saved file and audit the answer range

Saving without an error does **not** mean the values are right: the sandbox reports
`[Code executed successfully with no output]` for a file full of formulas, blanks, or `#N/A`.
The only evidence that your answer exists is reading it back out of the saved file.

Run this as its own round, after the save. Paste it, set the two constants, and read the
output:

```python
import datetime
from openpyxl import load_workbook
from openpyxl.utils import range_boundaries

# a date/time IS a valid stored value — it must not be mistaken for a formula object
SCALAR = (int, float, bool, str, datetime.datetime, datetime.date,
          datetime.time, datetime.timedelta)

OUT = "<output_path>"
INP = "<spreadsheet_path>"          # compared against, so nothing is silently erased
POS = "<answer_position>"           # e.g. "'Sheet1'!A14:E17" or "D2:D5"

sheet, rng = (POS.rsplit("!", 1) if "!" in POS else (None, POS))
if sheet:
    sheet = sheet.strip().strip("'")
wb = load_workbook(OUT, data_only=False)      # False: a formula shows up as its "=" text
ws = wb[sheet] if sheet else wb.active
c1, r1, c2, r2 = range_boundaries(rng.strip())

wi = load_workbook(INP, data_only=True)       # what Excel DISPLAYED in the input
si = None                                     # stays None when the answer sheet is NEW
if sheet is None:
    si = wi.active
elif sheet in wi.sheetnames:
    si = wi[sheet]

SHOW = 30                           # keep the printout readable on a big range
counts, defects, blanks, lost, shown = {}, [], [], [], 0
for row in ws.iter_rows(min_row=r1, max_row=r2, min_col=c1, max_col=c2):
    for c in row:
        v = c.value
        if v is None or (isinstance(v, str) and not v.strip()):
            kind = "BLANK"          # may be correct — see the checklist below
        elif not isinstance(v, SCALAR):
            kind = "FORMULA-OBJECT"          # ArrayFormula etc.
        elif isinstance(v, str) and v.startswith("="):
            kind = "FORMULA"
        elif isinstance(v, str) and v.startswith("#"):
            kind = "EXCEL-ERROR"
        else:
            kind = "ok"
        counts[kind] = counts.get(kind, 0) + 1
        # a value the INPUT displayed here but the output no longer has
        iv = si[c.coordinate].value if si is not None else None
        if iv is not None and kind == "BLANK" and len(lost) < SHOW:
            lost.append((c.coordinate, repr(iv)[:30]))
        if kind in ("FORMULA", "FORMULA-OBJECT", "EXCEL-ERROR") and len(defects) < SHOW:
            defects.append((c.coordinate, kind))      # always wrong
        elif kind == "BLANK" and len(blanks) < SHOW:
            blanks.append(c.coordinate)               # judge these, see below
        if shown < SHOW:            # a sample of what is actually stored, with types
            print(c.coordinate, repr(v)[:60], type(v).__name__, kind)
            shown += 1
print("COUNTS:", counts)
print("MUST-FIX:", defects)
print("ERASED (was a value, now blank — intended only if asked to clear):", lost)
print("BLANK cells (correct or not? decide per the instruction):", blanks)
```

Then judge what you see:

- any `FORMULA` / `FORMULA-OBJECT` → always a defect, **including a formula that came from the
  input and you never touched** (see Rule 1's "a formula the INPUT put there"). Replace it with
  a literal: its input cached value if the instruction leaves that cell alone, your own computed
  value if the instruction changes it.
- anything in `ERASED` → the input displayed a value there and your output does not. If the
  instruction asked you to **delete / clear / blank / remove** those cells, this list is your
  answer working and every entry is expected — leave it alone. Otherwise you destroyed a value,
  usually by saving a formula cell without its cached value or by a stray `None` assignment;
  restore it.
- any `EXCEL-ERROR` → your computation is wrong. Fix the logic, not the cell. Always a defect.
- values present but of the wrong type (a number stored as `str`, a date stored as text), or
  numbers that disagree with what you can check by hand from the input → recompute.
- a `BLANK` cell needs a judgement, not a reflex. It is **correct** when the instruction asked
  you to clear that cell, or when it lies past the end of the real data (`Sheet-Level` ranges
  are routinely larger than the answer, and padding rows are expected to stay empty). It is a
  **defect** only when the instruction supplies a value for it and you have none there — then
  find the cause (wrong sheet, wrong row offset, a stray `None`/`""` assignment) and fix it.
  Never fill a blank cell just to make the range look complete: inventing a value where the
  expected cell is empty loses exactly as much as leaving a real value out.
- also confirm the cells you were **not** asked to change still hold their original values —
  compare them against the same cells in `spreadsheet_path`.

If the audit finds a problem, fix it with **one complete replacement solution** that reads
`spreadsheet_path` and writes `output_path` from scratch. Do not patch the output file with a
follow-up snippet, and do not let the audit block itself write the file — it must only read.

When the audit is clean, stop. Do not resubmit code you have already run: a round that
re-executes an identical block learns nothing and changes nothing.

text:

Solve the spreadsheet manipulation task below. The fields mean:

- **instruction** — what the user wants done. It is written by a spreadsheet user, so it often
  asks for "a formula"; what is graded is the resulting **values**, so compute them in Python.
- **spreadsheet_path** — the input workbook. Read it; never modify it in place.
- **spreadsheet_content** — a `pandas.read_excel(..., header=0)` preview of each sheet. The
  column labels you see are the contents of **Excel row 1**, and preview row `i` is **Excel
  row i + 2**. Treat it as a hint about shape only, and confirm every real cell address by
  opening the file.
- **instruction_type** — `Cell-Level Manipulation`: `answer_position` is the exact cell(s) to
  fill. `Sheet-Level Manipulation`: `answer_position` is the **maximum** range you may modify,
  not a quota to fill.
- **answer_position** — the graded cell(s). When it carries a sheet name (`'Sheet1'!A2:A19`),
  write to **that sheet, selected by name**. Cells in this range that the instruction does not
  ask you to change must keep their original values.
- **output_path** — write the modified workbook to this exact path. Everything outside
  `answer_position` should be preserved as it was in the input.

## How to use your {max_turns} rounds

Reply with exactly **ONE** ```python fenced code block per round — only the FIRST block in
your reply is executed, so a reply with several blocks silently throws the rest away. Put
your reasoning in comments inside that one block. Its stdout (or its traceback) comes back to
you as the next message.

Work in this order, one round each:

1. **Inspect, and find the worked example.** Open `spreadsheet_path` and `print` what you
   actually need: the sheet names, and the real coordinates and values of the header row, the
   first data rows, and the cells in and around `answer_position`. Print each target cell
   **twice** — once with `data_only=True` (the value Excel displayed) and once with
   `data_only=False` (the formula text, if any) — so you know which cells arrive as formulas.
   Then look for the user's own worked example: cells already filled inside `answer_position`,
   and any labelled block (`The Result I'm after`, `Expected`, `Outcome`) elsewhere on the
   sheet. Nothing is graded this round, so look before you leap — guessing a header row or a
   label is the most common way these tasks are lost.
2. **Solve.** First state, in a comment, the rule you inferred and confirm it reproduces
   **every** example cell you found in step 1 — if it contradicts one, the rule is wrong, not
   the example. Then compute the answer values in Python and write them, as literals of the
   right type, to `answer_position`; save the workbook to `output_path`. Every cell in the
   range must end up a literal or a deliberate blank, including cells that arrived holding a
   formula — saving those unchanged drops their value and the grader reads them empty.
3. **Audit.** Re-open the **saved output file**, print every cell of `answer_position` with
   its value and Python type, and check each one against the same cell in `spreadsheet_path`.
   A formula string, a `#N/A`-style error token, or a wrong Python type is always a defect —
   a formula is a defect even if the input put it there and you left it alone, because saving
   it discarded the value Excel had cached. A blank cell where the **input** displayed a value
   is a defect unless you were asked to clear that cell. A blank is legitimate past the end of
   the real data and where the instruction asked you to clear a cell, so do not pad the range
   out to look full. Also confirm the cells you were not asked to change still hold their
   original values. This round must only READ — it must not write the output file.
4. **Correct if needed.** If the audit found a problem, send **one complete replacement
   solution** that reads `spreadsheet_path` and writes `output_path` from scratch, then audit
   again. Do not patch the existing output file with a partial snippet.

`[Code executed successfully with no output]` means only that nothing raised — it is not
evidence that your answer is correct or even present. The audit in step 3 is the only
evidence, so do not treat the task as finished before it comes back clean.

When the audit is clean, reply with a one-sentence summary and **no code block** — that ends
the task. Never resubmit a block you have already run unchanged: it cannot produce a new
result, and repeating it wastes rounds you could spend fixing a real defect.
